html:
Thomas Edison was an American inventor and businessman who gave the world the phonograph, a practical electric light bulb and a system to power it, and helped launch motion pictures. His biggest invention may have been the industrial research lab.

Born in Ohio and raised in Michigan, he had little schooling and lost much of his hearing as a child. He started as a telegraph operator and made his first money improving telegraph equipment.

In 1876 he set up a laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey, staffed by a team of machinists, chemists and engineers whose job was to invent on purpose. Out of it came:

  • the phonograph in 1877, the first machine to record and play back sound;
  • a long-lasting incandescent light bulb in 1879, after testing thousands of materials for the filament;
  • the first commercial power station, Pearl Street in New York, in 1882, sending direct current to paying customers;
  • with his staff, the Kinetoscope, an early movie viewer, in the 1890s.

He held 1,093 US patents. He fought a bitter "war of the currents" against the alternating current system backed by George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla, and lost; AC became the standard. His company became part of General Electric in 1892.

Edison belongs on the chart as part of the second wave of industrialisation, when electricity, the telephone and recorded sound changed daily life. His friend Henry Ford started as an engineer at an Edison company.
